Croft.meta: UX/UI Design & Product Strategy • Case study
Croft.title: Building a design system for high data density dashboards
Croft.overviewText: Each product in the company had its own visual identity, with different component libraries and no common vocabulary. I was primarily responsible for creating a design system from scratch for well data monitoring products and scientific applications, unifying tokens, components, and documentation. The result was visual consistency across systems, a living documentation that became a reference for new screens, and a real reduction in delivery time: screens that took 3 to 4 days to prototype were now done in 1 to 2 days.
Croft.problemText1: There was no visual standard between the products. Each application used a different library, with no harmony in colors, spacing, or typography. This led to products that looked like they belonged to different companies, and constant rework: each new screen was a design decision made from scratch, with no defined tokens or shared criteria for what was right.
Croft.processText1: Listening to those who would use the system.
Croft.processDesc1: Before designing any token, I talked to the front-end team to understand what they really needed. This conversation shaped the priorities: which components had the most friction in implementation and where the biggest maintenance pains were.
Croft.processDesc2: I prioritized the most used components across all company systems, not the most beautiful or complex ones, but what would bring visual consistency fastest to the largest number of products.
Croft.processDesc3: I used Tailwind as a reference for naming and MUI as an aesthetic reference for some components, adapting both to the context of data-dense dashboards, aimed at a technical and scientific audience.
Croft.processDesc4: The documentation was built in Figma (specs and guidelines for the design team) and in Storybook (living components for the front-end). Keeping both synchronized was as much a part of the job as designing the components.
Croft.decision1Title: 1. A broad palette was a necessity, not a luxury
Croft.decision1Text: Well monitoring dashboards represent many simultaneous variables, with multiple curves overlapping on the same chart. This required a much broader palette than usual, both for the initial templates and for color suggestions in the customization forms, where the user themselves chooses how to view their data.
Croft.decision2Text: My first decision was to avoid colors with variable opacity, to maintain full control without depending on what was behind each element. In practice, opacity proved to be the most practical way to handle interaction states like hover and pressed, without needing to manually define a color for each state on every surface of the system. It was one of the decisions I most needed to unlearn in the project.
Croft.decision3Text: The product is aimed at dashboards and forms, not editorial content. Because of this, I opted for a compact typographic scale, which kept the interface predictable and reduced unnecessary decisions when using the design system.
Croft.beforeText: Fragmented design with no established visual standard.
Croft.afterText: Unified interface with the new Design System, cleaner and more consistent.
Croft.impact1: Visual consistency across products that previously seemed to be from different companies.
Croft.impact2: Living documentation in Figma and Storybook, used as a reference in daily work.
Croft.impact3: Screens that took 3 to 4 days to prototype were now done in 1 to 2 days, with high fidelity and animated interactions.
Croft.impact4: For simpler screens, the front-end team started prototyping directly in code, with design support, something only possible because the design system was already reliable enough to sustain this workflow.

DepthTrack.title: Depth Track
DepthTrack.subtitle: Redesigning the depth track of a well drilling dashboard
DepthTrack.usersVal: petroleum engineers, petrophysicists, data engineers, control room operators, drilling engineers, rig operators, and supervisors
DepthTrack.contextText: STRATVISION displays drilling curves (ROP, WOB, Gamma Ray, gases) along the well depth in real-time. The depth track seems like the simplest element of the dashboard. But the correct reading of the rest of the screen depends entirely on it.
DepthTrack.problemText1: Testing the software at the 1:25 scale, the depth ticks were so far apart that the track became a practically empty space. Like zooming way in on a real ruler: only the space between the marks remains.
DepthTrack.problemText2: Result: at closer scales, the user lost their sense of location in the well.
DepthTrack.quote: "I saw that the depths disappeared when changing the scale, but I thought it only bothered me."
DepthTrack.prototypeText: I took the first prototype (Figma) to developers for testing. Each person tried a different interaction without me explaining anything: click and drag to navigate, click on the center column to change scale. I incorporated each of these findings into the component.
DepthTrack.structureDesc1: — the entire well, marking the visible section
DepthTrack.structureDesc3: — zoom of the selected section, with more indicators
DepthTrack.missingTitle: 5. The missing moment: "And then, what do I do?"
DepthTrack.missingText: A test group simply froze in front of the component. This question showed me that the interaction was not self-explanatory to everyone. I created a floating legend, inspired by game HUDs, that appears on hover and explains each available gesture.
DepthTrack.resultText: Immediate adoption, no training needed. The component was added to the product's design system, ready for reuse on other screens.
DepthTrack.learningsText: Not every UX problem comes in as a complaint; sometimes it's just silently tolerated. And the fastest way to discover the right interaction is to put the prototype in front of real people as soon as possible.

IfSolve.title: What 51 usability problems taught me about truly looking at an interface

toc.takeaways: 5. What I take from this project

IfSolve.startText1: This project never seemed simple. It was the first time I did a complete heuristic evaluation of a software, not just an isolated screen as a class exercise. IFSolve is an online test and questions system used by students and teachers, and the work involved going through the entire experience: login, test creation, question registration, and answering tests.
IfSolve.startText2: Compared to previous exercises, the difference was clear. I wasn't analyzing a ready-made snapshot; I needed to see the entire system, understand the usage context of each screen, and most importantly, justify each problem found with a concrete guideline.
IfSolve.challengeText1: The project was part of college, developed among students and supervised by guiding professors. My role was to navigate each screen of the system like a real user would, compare what I found with a list of usability guidelines (the Eureca List, by Matos and Freire, 2023), and document each deviation clearly enough so that any team member could understand the problem and its severity.
IfSolve.challengeText2: In the end, the report gathered 51 guideline violations, organized by screen, violated principle, and severity (critical, severe, moderate, mild).
IfSolve.processDesc: I separated the process into three steps that I now use as a personal baseline for any heuristic evaluation:
IfSolve.processItem1: 1. Map the journey, not just the screens.
IfSolve.processDesc1: I went through the entire flow—login, test creation, question registration, answering, and viewing results—as if I were a real student trying to finish a test.
IfSolve.processItem2: 2. Confront each screen with the guidelines list.
IfSolve.processDesc2: Each finding became a "GV" (Guideline Violation), always with the same structure: problem description, correction suggestion, violated principle, and severity. This formatting discipline is what made the report truly useful, not just a list of opinions.
IfSolve.processDesc3: Having 51 points doesn't mean the system is bad; it means we could separate signal from noise. This taught me to resist the temptation to "stack problems" and focus on communicating what really blocks the user.
IfSolve.findingsItem1Desc: The search field at the top of the system performed no action when triggered, despite looking like a functional element. Classified as critical, this type of failure compromises a basic functionality expected in any search bar.
IfSolve.findingsItem2Desc: Closing the tab during test creation resulted in the loss of all entered content, with no prior warning or recovery option. Classified as severe, this problem generates direct rework for whoever is filling out the form.
IfSolve.findingsItem3Desc: The text field intended for discursive answers had no border or background color, which compromised its visibility as a data entry area.
IfSolve.findingsItem4Title: Lack of feedback when submitting an incomplete test.
IfSolve.findingsItem4Desc: The system allowed the submission of a test without any questions answered, without displaying any warning message. Classified as critical, this type of feedback absence can result in the improper submission of incomplete tests.
IfSolve.takeawaysTitle: 5. What I take from this project
IfSolve.takeawaysText1: I didn't know heuristic evaluation before this project. The person who introduced me to the method was professor Silva Matos, author of the Eureca List itself used in the evaluation, and so I arrived without any preconceived idea of how the process should work. This turned out to be good: I learned the method while applying it, without prejudices about what I "should" find or how to classify each problem.
IfSolve.takeawaysText2: Over time, I realized that the real value of the evaluation lies in translating perception into argument: it's not enough to feel that something is wrong; you need to name the principle, measure the severity, and propose a solution path that someone else can execute without needing to ask you anything.
IfSolve.takeawaysText3: It was also the project that taught me not to confuse volume with depth. A 51-point report is only useful if someone can open it and, in five minutes, know exactly what to solve first.
